title: D.E.B.S.
full_review:
Discipline. Energy. Beauty. Strength. Those are some of the attributes it takes to join the underground secret agents known as D.E.B.S. Those, and the ability to lie, cheat and fight, that is.

"D.E.B.S." (Destination/Samuel Goldwyn) is a satire of the "Charlie's Angels" genre of action films and also of teen movies, though here the protagonists are high school seniors who know how to pack a punch.

When they take on the archcriminal Lucy Diamond (Jordana Brewster), it's pretty much business as usual for these stories. But hold on, there's a surprising twist:

Blonde honor-student Amy (Sara Foster), one of the leading D.E.B.S., has just broken up with her boyfriend. And when she comes face to face with the deadly Lucy, weapons drawn, instead of killing her, Amy begins to feel the stirrings of a romantic attraction, which sends her into an emotional tailspin. This is fine with the predatory Lucy, who plainly likes girls, and clearly feels something special with Amy.

Though at first resolutely stifling her inclinations, Amy eventually lets herself go. Before long, the two former adversaries share a romantic idyll (nothing terribly graphic, but some amorous tussling on a bed).

There's also a more conventional subplot involving the timid Janet (Jill Ritchie) who falls for Lucy's (male) sidekick. The other D.E.B.S. include leader Max (Meagan Good), who temporarily loses her command position to Amy, and boy-crazy Domique (Devon Aoki).

The girls report to headmistress Mrs. Peatree (Holland Taylor) and D.E.B.S. president Phipps (Michael Clarke Duncan) who can both magically materialize when they need to give orders to their charges or reprimand them, as the case may be.

Director and writer Angela Robinson's lesbian riff on a familiar genre -- surprisingly slick for an independent film -- is not without bright moments, and there are some appealing performances.

But, despite imparting some worthy messages such as the value of friendship and being true to yourself, the ringing affirmation of giving physical vent to one's sexuality, gay or straight, particularly at the borderline age of consent, is troubling, even if presented in the context of a lighthearted spoof. (In addition to the Amy-Lucy pairing, Domique chronically has a boy in her bed after curfew.)

The film contains some profane, rough and crude language, action violence, premarital sexual situations, overall thematic material, and alcohol and tobacco use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
